title: The great vehicle
hook: the name the Mahayana gave itself; Buddhists today avoid the old contrast term and say Theravada instead

segments.voice: Yesterday, the higher teaching folded up: mind, factors, matter, conditions. Your line: the smallest parts. Which list did you keep, and did you use it? Today a new block begins. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

A big old house is on fire, and the father is outside. His children are still in there, playing, too absorbed to notice the smoke. He shouts, and they don't come. So he tries something else. He calls out that he has carts waiting at the gate, the kind they've always wanted: a cart pulled by goats, one by deer, one by an ox. The children come running out. And when they're safe, he doesn't give them those three. He gives each child one great cart, finer than any of them asked for. That story comes from the Lotus Sutra. Its word for those carts is the word in today's name.
screen: `A HOUSE ON FIRE.` → `THREE CARTS AT THE GATE.` → `ONE GREAT CART FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: First, the vehicle. The Sanskrit word is yana: a cart, a vehicle, the thing that carries you somewhere. Buddhist teachers used it for a path, the way across. In the Lotus Sutra's parable, the three carts stand for different paths of practice, and the one great cart for the single vehicle the sutra says they all lead into. Second, the name. Communities who treasured sutras like the Lotus called their way Mahayana. Maha means great. The great vehicle, wide enough to carry all beings. That's the name they gave themselves, and it's the name used here. Third, the hard part. Some Mahayana texts also used a contrast term for other paths: a lesser, or small, vehicle. It was a word for someone else, not a name anyone took for themselves. The Buddhists of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia call their own tradition Theravada, the way of the elders, a name this path met long ago. Buddhists today avoid the old contrast term and say Theravada instead. So this path will too, and when the old term shows up in a text, it's there as history. Fourth, what that habit teaches. A name someone gives you can carry a judgment inside it. A name you give yourself carries what you love. Mahayana Buddhists, Theravada Buddhists, and the many schools ahead on this path, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions, will each be called here by the name they use. No ranking, just each by its own name.
screen: `YANA: A CART, A WAY ACROSS.` · `MAHA: GREAT. THE GREAT VEHICLE.` · `AN OLD CONTRAST WORD, SET DOWN.` · then, large: `EACH BY ITS OWN NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: use each one's own name. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a few people you know, one at a time. For each, notice the name you use for them in your head. Is it the name they'd use for themselves? A nickname they never liked? A label, like the difficult one, or the neighbor? Gently swap it for the name they'd choose. Say it silently, and let their face come with it. Then breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Mahayana. The great vehicle: the name these communities gave their own way, wide enough to carry all beings. Today's word.
Your line: each by its own name. Today, when you speak of a group of people, use the name they use for themselves. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Mahayana is the name used for the Buddhist traditions of China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Tibet, among others; Buddhists today refer to the tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia as Theravada.

fork.setup: your children are playing in a burning house and won't come out when you shout. what does the father in the Lotus Sutra do?
options: run in and carry them out one by one
promise the carts they've always wanted
fork.reveal: he promises goat, deer and ox carts at the gate. they come running, and then he gives each one great cart instead.

original.note: Sanskrit: maha, great, and yana, vehicle. the great vehicle.

trapdoor: what you thought: the bigger branch of Buddhism.
what it means: the name these communities gave their own way, a vehicle wide enough to carry all beings.
what a scholar hears: yana as in the Lotus Sutra's carts; a contrast term for other paths appears in some Mahayana texts, and Buddhists today set it aside and say Theravada.

sources.ref: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), chapter 3, the parable of the burning house (Kern, SBE XXI, 1884)

notes: The burning-house parable is paraphrased from Kern's 1884 translation (chapter 3); Kern's wording was not quoted. In some versions the three carts are drawn by goats, deer and oxen; confirm.
The old contrast term (hinayana) is described but deliberately not spoken, per the outline. Confirm a Keeper is happy with that choice, or prefers it named once as history.
Countries listed for Theravada (Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia) repeat day 291's index line.
'Maha means great' and 'yana: a cart, a vehicle' are standard dictionary glosses, given in the original-word note; confirm.
howItsDone lists Mahayana countries with 'among others'; Tibetan Buddhism is often counted as Mahayana and also called Vajrayana. Confirm wording.
